canonical_question: How does the 'partial sintering' method using SPS lower the cost and time compared to the conventional full consolidation method used by Kim et al.?

question_variants.question: How does the 'partial sintering' method specifically lower the cost and time compared to the conventional full consolidation used by Kim et al.?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The document states that the partial sintering method using spark plasma sintering (SPS) lowers the time and cost of processing, but it does not provide a specific quantitative comparison to the conventional full consolidation method used by Kim et al., nor does it detail the specific mechanisms (e.g., shorter time, lower temperature, reduced steps) that differentiate the two methods in a direct comparison.

answers.answer: The paper mentions that the CuMoTaWV target was partially sintered at 1000 °C using SPS specifically to lower the cost and time of target preparation, but it does not elaborate on the specific comparative details against the full consolidation method used by Kim et al.
answers.measurement_outcome: Lower cost and time of target preparation claimed
answers.boundary_limitation: No direct quantitative comparison data provided against Kim et al. method
evidence_spans: A single target containing the principal elements, CuMoTaWV, was partially sintered at 1000 °C using SPS to lower the cost and time of target preparation, as shown in Figure 1 .
The elemental maps from the cross section of the target in Figure 1 b showed a uniform distribution of all of the elemental phases.
This suggests that in the DC sputter film from the single target, the plasma will evaporate all of the principal elements to the substrate.

cross_paper_synthesis.consensus: The use of a 'partial sintering' method at 1000 °C via Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) for the CuMoTaWV alloy is explicitly claimed to reduce the cost and time of target preparation.
cross_paper_synthesis.different_approaches: The available evidence relies on a single source (PMC7304825) which describes the partial sintering strategy as a cost/time-saving measure but does not provide the direct methodological comparison or quantitative data against the conventional full consolidation method attributed to Kim et al.
cross_paper_synthesis.condition_dependencies: The cost and time reduction is specifically linked to the 'partially sintered' state achieved at 1000 °C using SPS.
cross_paper_synthesis.evidence_strength: The claim of efficiency is stated but lacks the quantitative backing or direct comparative data found in the full consolidation method to verify the extent of the improvement.
cross_paper_synthesis.unresolved_gap: There is a missing regime of direct quantitative comparison data between the partial sintering approach and the conventional full consolidation method used by Kim et al., preventing a definitive assessment of the magnitude of time and cost savings.
cross_paper_synthesis.candidate_hypothesis: Partial sintering likely bypasses the energy and time requirements of complete densification, thereby reducing processing time, though the specific duration required to reach the 'partially sintered' state is not quantified in the provided text.
cross_paper_synthesis.discriminating_experiment: A comparative experiment should be conducted to measure the exact sintering duration required to achieve the 'partially sintered' state at 1000 °C and directly compare the total processing time and energy consumption against a full consolidation run following Kim et al.'s protocol.
